title: Wise and Foolish Side by Side
overview: This chapter opens a long collection of short sayings that set the wise, honest life beside the foolish, crooked one, especially in how people handle work, money and words.

parts.label: A new collection begins (v. 1)
parts.note: The book shifts here from longer speeches to short sayings, most of them two lines that contrast a good path with a bad one. The first says children's choices shape their parents' happiness, and naming father and mother is likely a poetic way of meaning both parents.

parts.label: Money, honesty and work (vv. 2-5)
parts.note: Wealth gained by cheating brings no lasting good, while honest and generous living protects a person, and the LORD is said to keep the righteous fed and block the cravings of the wicked. Verses 4 and 5 praise steady work at the right time, like bringing in the harvest while the season lasts.

parts.label: Reputation and integrity (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: Good people are remembered with blessing, while a wicked person's name will 'rot,' meaning it decays into disgrace or is forgotten. The sly wink in verse 10 signals a hidden scheme, and the thread running through is that crooked living eventually comes to light while honest words give life like a fountain.

parts.label: Love, words and silence (vv. 12-21)
parts.note: Hatred keeps quarrels alive, but love 'covers over' wrongs by forgiving them rather than exposing them, a line later echoed in the New Testament. Many of these sayings warn that talking too much invites trouble, while careful words are like choice silver and can 'nourish' many people.

parts.label: What lasts and what doesn't (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: Those who respect the LORD are pictured standing firm, while the wicked are swept away like debris after a storm. Many readers take these as observations about how life tends to go rather than promises for every case, a tension that other biblical books such as Job openly wrestle with.

parts.label: Speech that bears fruit (vv. 31-32)
parts.note: The chapter closes on speech again: the words of good people produce wisdom the way a healthy plant bears fruit. Twisted talk, by contrast, will be 'silenced.'

disagreement: Christians differ on whether sayings like these promise that faithful people will prosper and live long, or describe general patterns that real life often breaks.
think: When have you seen honesty pay off over time, and when has it seemed to cost someone, and what do you make of the difference?
